critique.good: 股票代码和行情数值保持完整，价格、涨跌幅和成交额列便于纵向比较。
critique.problems: 名称和行业都逐字竖排，表头尤其高，几乎每行也被拉高；数值列因此出现大块空白，横向追踪同一股票的行情很费力。
critique.cause: 名称和行业各为53px，扣除内边距后不足以并排容纳两个汉字；市盈率60px也使表头换行。

critique.good: 名称大多按两个字一行排列，明显改善股票识别和行的紧凑度；代码及数值保持完整，行情列易于比较。
critique.problems: 行业仍逐字竖排，四字行业使末行很高；行业表头也占四行，造成表头和数值列上方大量空白。
critique.cause: 65px的名称列能容纳两个汉字，但41px的行业列只能容纳一个汉字；市盈率列也不足以让表头保持一行。

critique.good: 行业大多能按两个字一行阅读，行业表头也比其他两个方案紧凑；代码和数值保持完整。
critique.problems: 名称逐字竖排，主要股票标识难以快速辨认，多数数据行随之增高，行情列留下大片空白。
critique.cause: 41px的名称列只能容纳一个汉字，而65px分给行业列后，名称没有足够宽度并排显示两个汉字。

critique.good: 代码和行情数值完整，便于按股票定位并纵向比较；名称大多每行显示两个汉字。
critique.problems: 行业表头竖排成四行，行业名称也逐字堆叠，拉高表头和部分数据行，削弱了横向读行的节奏。市盈率表头也被拆成两行。
critique.cause: 行业列宽50px，仅有29px文字空间，容不下两个17px汉字；市盈率列宽60px，仅有39px文字空间，容不下三字表头。

critique.good: 代码和数值仍保持完整，名称列有较宽的文字空间。
critique.problems: 整体高度和行高与r1A相同；行业表头和行业名称依然逐字堆叠，名称列增加的宽度没有改善实际换行。
critique.cause: 名称列从56px增至60px，仍主要按两个汉字一行显示；行业列缩至46px，仍只能容纳一个汉字。

critique.good: 代码和行情数值保持完整，股票可以准确定位，价格、涨跌幅等数值也便于纵向比较。成交额表头分行后仍能辨认。
critique.problems: 名称和所属行业多数逐字竖排，使各行过高，同行数值下方出现大量空白；名称尤其难以作为股票标识快速识别。市盈率表头也被拆开，行业表头占据四行。
critique.cause: 名称列宽51px、行业列宽55px，扣除21px内边距和边框后都不足以并排容纳两个约18px的汉字。市盈率列宽60px，容纳完整表头所需的宽度不足。

r0A.idea: 均衡分配名称和行业宽度，保留所有代码与数值的完整显示，让两列文本共同承担换行。

r0B.idea: 优先保证股票名称的可读性，适合先按名称定位个股，但行业列会更频繁地换行。

r0C.idea: 优先展示行业分类，适合按行业浏览和比较，但股票名称会更频繁地换行。

r1A.idea: 以r0B为基础，将名称列缩至56px，腾出9px给行业列。目标是保留名称每行两个汉字，同时尝试让行业列也容纳两个汉字；需通过渲染确认实际字宽是否允许。

r1B.idea: 保留较宽的名称列，从r0B转移5px给行业列。若更激进的平衡方案使名称退回逐字换行，此方案可优先维持股票名称的可读性，并减少行业列的拥挤。

r2A.idea: 将名称列缩至51px，把行业列增至55px。行业列可尝试每行容纳两个汉字，改善四字行业表头和较长行业名称；代价是股票名称可能逐字换行。保留代码和各数值列所需宽度，便于与现有方案比较两种文本分配。

r3A.idea: 将行业列的6px移给名称列，使名称可按两个汉字一行排列，改善股票识别并缩短多行；行业仍可能逐字排列，但保留所有代码和数值的完整宽度。

r3B.idea: 将名称列的2px移给行业列，使行业可按两个汉字一行排列，改善分类信息和行业表头的阅读；名称仍可能逐字排列，适合更重视行业比较的场景。

understanding.purpose: 展示部分A股个股行情，供读者按股票比较价格、涨跌、成交额、估值和所属行业。
understanding.reading: 读者先用代码或名称定位股票，再沿行读取行情；纵向扫描数值列可比较不同股票。名称和行业换行会增加部分行高，这些行的空白也可容纳同一行其他文本换行。
groups: 代码、名称：共同标识股票，代码是精确查找的关键。
最新价、涨跌幅：共同描述当前价格及其变化。
成交额（亿）、市盈率：分别提供交易规模和估值信息，都是用于纵向比较的数值列。
所属行业：提供股票分类，便于结合行情理解和比较。
keep_intact: 股票代码及各列完整数值，包括小数点、正负号、百分号和千位分隔符。
may_wrap: 股票名称和所属行业可在汉字间换行，但应保持同一单元格内的词语易读。
较长表头可换行，尤其是成交额（亿）；表头行高度可容纳这种换行。

bad.why: Stock names and industries both become predominantly one character per line, making rows unusually tall and identifiers difficult to scan.
Stock names run vertically, weakening the connection between each company and its prices despite the more readable industry column.
Both descriptive columns are too narrow for comfortable reading, producing long vertical strings and excessive empty space in the numeric columns.
The name column forces company names into vertical strings, making the principal row identifiers harder to recognize.

final.rationale: r1A keeps stock codes and market figures intact while allowing company names to read in two-character groups. Its industry column is narrow, but allocating more width to it would force the more important company names into vertical strings. The resulting row heights give the numeric values a more consistent rhythm than the alternatives that stack names character by character.

general: Protect row identifiers and numeric values so readers can recognize entries and compare figures across rows.
Judge wrapping by its effect on reading and row rhythm, not just by table height or the number of wrapped headers.
specific: At this viewport width, the available space cannot keep all names, industries and numeric values on one line.
Giving the name column at least 56px preserves two-character groupings in the rendered candidates, while industry labels take the remaining narrow column.

final.tradeoffs: A wider industry column makes sectors easier to read but leaves company names vertical; a wider name column offers slightly more breathing room while narrowing the already constrained industry column.
final.uncertain: The ranges describe the observed preferred family, not a tested guarantee for every intermediate width. Name and industry widths must be adjusted together to stay within 495px; the endpoints of both ranges cannot be used simultaneously.

A.why: Codes and numeric values remain intact, and company names mostly read in two-character chunks. The very narrow industry column stacks characters vertically, making that field and its header hard to scan.

B.why: Stock codes, prices and percentages break across lines, disrupting the identifiers and figures readers need to compare. Several headers also fragment awkwardly.

C.why: Codes and numbers stay intact, but company names and industries run mostly one character per line. The resulting tall rows make it harder to connect each name with its figures.

D.why: As in C, intact numbers come at the expense of vertically stacked company names and industries. Tall rows and fragmented labels slow scanning.

E.why: Codes and figures remain on one line, while company names usually wrap into readable chunks. The industry column is still only one character wide, producing a fragmented header and tall final rows.

F.why: Codes and numeric values stay intact, and company names mostly wrap into two-character chunks. Industry labels stack vertically, though their column has slightly more breathing room than in E.

reviews.unsure: A, E and F are very close visually; small differences in their column widths make the choice between them marginal. All three leave the industry column uncomfortably narrow.

A.why: Codes and financial values remain intact, and names mostly read in two-character chunks. The industry column is only one character wide, making its header and longer entries difficult to scan.

B.why: Identifiers and numbers stay intact, but names wrap into short fragments and the industry column reads one character per line. The narrow name column also makes the table feel cramped.

C.why: Codes, prices and percentages split across lines, breaking the identifiers and numeric values readers need to compare. Several headers also fragment awkwardly.

D.why: Financial values remain intact, but both company names and industries run vertically one character at a time. Tall rows and empty numeric cells weaken the connection across each row.

E.why: Codes and financial values are readable, but company names and industries are forced into vertical character stacks. The resulting tall rows make comparisons across the table laborious.

F.why: Codes and numbers stay intact, and company names generally wrap in readable two-character chunks. The one-character-wide industry column remains a major scanning problem.

reviews.unsure: A and F are very close visually; their small differences in column proportions do not clearly outweigh the shared problem of the narrow industry column.
